en: *Recorded Sayings of the Disciples from Various Directions*, Scroll II (Combined with the *Essential Treatise on Sudden Enlightenment*).
When the Master first arrived in Jiangxi to visit Mazu, Mazu asked him, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Dayun Temple in Yuezhou.
Mazu asked, "What do you intend to seek by coming here? He said, "I have come to seek the Buddha-dharma. Mazu said, "The precious treasury is within yourself."
[The Master] did not look back. [The monk asked], "Why do you abandon your home and flee? Here I have nothing at all; what Buddha-dharma would you seek?
The Master then prostrated and asked, "Which one is the precious treasury of Huihai himself? The Patriarch said, "That which is now asking me is your own precious treasury.
It is fully complete with everything; there is nothing lacking. Its use is entirely free and spontaneous."
"Why should one falsely seek outside? At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment; he realized his own original mind without relying on intellectual cognition.
Leaping for joy, he prostrated in gratitude and served as a disciple for six years. Later, because his preceptor had grown old, he returned home abruptly to provide for him.

Thereupon, he concealed his traces and hid his capabilities, outwardly appearing dull and mute. He himself composed the *Tunwu rudao yaomen lun* (Treatise on the Essential Gate to Sudden Enlightenment and Entry into the Way), one scroll. The Dharma...
The Master’s disciple, his nephew Xuanyan, secretly traveled outside the Yangtze River to present himself to Mazu.

After Mazu had finished reading [the letter], he said to the assembly, “In Yuezhou there is a Great Pearl, perfectly round and bright, its light penetrating through; it is free and at ease, with no place of obstruction. Among the assembly was one who knew the Master’s surname was Zhu;
they took turns recommending him to one another, and having formed a bond, they went to Yuezhou to seek him out and rely upon him. At that time, he was called Dazhu Huairang.
Shangye (the master’s name was Huikai; he was a native of Jianzhou and studied under the monk Daozhi of Daoyun Temple in Yue).
The master said to his disciples, "I do not understand Chan, nor do I possess a single dharma to show to others. Therefore, there is no need for you to stand here for long; go and rest for now.
At that time, the number of students gradually increased, and they pressed him with their inquiries day and night. Finding himself unable to refuse them, he said:
He answered each question as it was posed, his eloquence being unimpeded. At that time, several Dharma masters came to visit him and said, "We intend to pose a question;
will you respond to us, Master? The Master replied, "The moon’s reflection in a deep pool—can one grasp it at will? They asked, "What is the Buddha?
The Master said, "In this clear discourse face-to-face, who else could it be but the Buddha? The assembly was left bewildered. (Fayan said, "This is precisely...")
After a long silence, the monk asked again, "What Dharma does the Master teach to save people? The Master replied, "I have never had a single Dharma to save people.
The monk said, "The houses of Chan masters are all like this. The Master then asked in return, "What Dharma do you, Virtuous One, teach to save people?
He replied, "I lecture on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The Master asked, "For how many sessions have you been lecturing? He replied, "Twenty."
The Master asked, "Who preached this sutra? The monk raised his voice and said, "Master, you are mocking me!
Do you not know that it was preached by the Buddha? The Master replied, "If one says that the Tathāgata has preached any dharma, they slander the Buddha;
such a person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught. If one says that this sutra was not preached by the Buddha, then they slander the sutra. [He requested...]
The Great Virtue was asked to look at it. The monk had no reply. After a short while, the Master asked again: "The Sutra says:
'If one sees me by form, or seeks me by sound, this person follows a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata. Great Virtue, tell me: which of these is the Tathāgata?
He replied, "When I reached this point, I became lost. The Master said, "You have never awakened from the beginning. What is there to talk about?"

The monk said, "I have forgotten my delusion. The monk asked, "Please, Zen Master, explain this for me. The Master said, "Great Virtue, you have lectured on the sutras more than twenty times, yet you do not recognize the Tathāgata.
The monk bowed again and requested, "I pray that you will grant me instruction. The Master said, "The Tathāgata is the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all dharmas.
How could you have forgotten this? The monk replied, "Yes, it is the meaning of the suchness of all dharmas. The Master said, "Great Virtue, it is you."
[The Master] said, "That too is not it. [The monk] asked, "The scriptural text is explicit; how can you say it is not? The Master said, "Virtuous One, is 'suchness' (tathatā) such?

[The monk] replied, "It is such. The Master said, "Are wood and stone such? [The monk] replied, "They are such. The Master said, "Virtuous One, are 'suchness' and 'wood and stone such' not two? [The monk] replied, "There is no duality.
The Master said, "What difference is there between the Virtuous One and wood and stone? The monk had no reply. Thereupon, [the Master] sighed and said, "This superior man..."
He was unable to offer a reply. After a long silence, he asked again, "How does one attain Great Nirvāṇa?
The Master said, "By not creating the karma of birth and death. The monk asked, "What is the karma of birth and death? The Master said, "Seeking Great Nirvāṇa is the karma of birth and death.

Abandoning defilement to grasp purity is the karma of birth and death. Having attainment and realization is the karma of birth and death. It is not to be free from the gate of counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*)."
"This is the karma of birth and death. [The monk] asked, "How then can one attain liberation? The Master said, "Originally there has been no bondage, so there is no need to seek liberation.
To proceed directly and act directly—this is the peerless equality. The monk said, "A Master such as you, Reverend, is truly rare indeed.
He paid his respects and departed.
A practitioner asked, "Regarding the saying 'this very mind is Buddha,' which one is the Buddha? The Master said, "Which one do you doubt is not the Buddha?
Point it out and show me. The practitioner had no reply. The Master said, "To realize it is for everything to be the realm; if you do not awaken, you will remain forever estranged."
The Vinaya Master Faming said to the Master, "The Chan masters' school mostly falls into emptiness. The Master replied, "In fact, it is the scholars' school that mostly falls into emptiness.
Faming was greatly startled and asked, "How can they fall into emptiness? The Master said, "The scriptures and treatises are but paper, ink, and characters;
since paper, ink, and characters are all empty, even if one establishes dharmas such as names and phrases upon sounds, they too are non-existent."

"It is not that this is empty," [the Master] said. "The Head of the Monastery (Zezhu) clings to the substance of the teachings; how could he not fall into emptiness? Faming asked, "Does the Chan Master fall into emptiness?
The Master replied, "I do not fall into emptiness. Faming asked, "Why is it that you do not fall into emptiness? The Master said, "Syllables and texts all arise from wisdom.
When the Great Function manifests before one, how could one fall into emptiness? Faming said, "Thus I know that one who does not penetrate even a single dharma..."
[The monk] did not call him Siddhārtha. The Master said, "The Vinaya Master has not only fallen into emptiness, but has also misused terminology.
Faming asked, pointing at his own form, "Where is the error? The Master said, "The Vinaya Master has not yet distinguished between the sounds of China and India;
how can he preach the Dharma? Faming said, "I request the Chan Master to point out my error. The Master said, "Do you not know that 'Siddhārtha' is..."

"In Sanskrit, yes. Although the Vinaya Master had reflected upon his transgression, his mind remained indignant. (The full Sanskrit is *Sarvārthasiddha*; in the Central Kingdom [China] it is translated as "All Meanings Accomplished.
The old rendering "Siddhārtha" is a corruption and abbreviation of the full term. He asked again, "The Sūtras, Vinayas, and Śāstras are the words of the Buddha.
One recites them and practices according to the teachings; why then do you not see your nature? The Master said, "It is like a mad dog chasing a clod of earth, while a lion bites a man."
The Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma constitute its essential function; those who read and recite them constitute its essential dharma.
Faming further asked: "Does Amitābha Buddha have parents and a clan? The Master replied: "Amitābha’s clan is Kauśika; his father’s name is Candrottarā."
The mother’s name was Shusheng Miaoyan (Exquisite and Wondrous Countenance). [Fa Ming] asked, "In which scriptural text does this appear? The Master replied, "It appears in the *Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha*.
Fa Ming paid his respects, withdrew, and departed with words of praise.
A Tripiṭaka Master asked, "Does True Suchness undergo change? The Master replied, "It does undergo change. The Tripiṭaka Master said, "Zen Master, you are mistaken.
The Master then asked the Tripiṭaka Master in return, "Do you possess True Suchness? He replied, "I do. The Master said, "If it does not undergo change, then you are certainly just an ordinary monk.
Have you not heard that a Good Friend (Kalyāṇamitra) can transform the three poisons into the Three Jewels?"
He gathers pure precepts; he transforms the six consciousnesses into the six supernormal powers; he transforms afflictions into bodhi; he transforms ignorance into great wisdom.
If True Suchness were subject to change, then the Tripitaka would truly be a naturalistic heresy. The Tripitaka Master said, "If that is so, then True Suchness must possess change.
The Master replied, "If one clings to the notion that True Suchness possesses change, that too is [an error]."
The outsider said, “Master, you just now said that True Suchness undergoes change, yet now you say it does not change.
How can this be the definitive truth? The Master replied, “If one clearly perceives one’s nature, it is like a mani jewel manifesting colors.”

It is permissible to speak of transformation, and it is also permissible to speak of non-transformation. Those who have not seen their own nature, upon hearing that True Suchness undergoes transformation, understand it as being subject to change;
upon hearing that it is unchanging, they understand it as being immutable. The Tripitaka Master said: "Therefore, one knows that the Southern School is truly unfathomable."
A practitioner of the Way asked, "Is there any phenomenon in the world that surpasses spontaneity (*ziran*)? The Master said, "There is. The practitioner asked, "What phenomenon can surpass it?
The Master said, "One who is able to know spontaneity. The practitioner asked, "Is primordial qi (*yuanqi*) the Way? The Master said, "Primordial qi is simply primordial qi."
The Master said, "The Way is simply the Way. [The monk] asked, "If it is thus, then there ought to be two. The Master said, "Know that there are not two people.
He asked again, "What is called 'deviant' and what is called 'correct'? The Master said, "When the mind pursues external objects, it is deviant; when objects follow the mind, it is correct."
The Vinaya Master Youyuan came to inquire, "Master, when you cultivate the Way, do you still apply effort? The Master replied, "I apply effort.
[The Master] asked, "How do you apply effort? The Master said, "When hungry, I eat; when weary, I sleep. [The Master] said, "All people do exactly this."
"Does your teacher apply himself with the same diligence? The Master replied, "No. The monk asked, "Why does he not do so? The Master said, "When he eats, he refuses to eat;
he demands a hundred kinds of things. When he sleeps, he refuses to sleep; he devises a thousand schemes. That is why he is different.
Thereupon, the Vinaya Master remained speechless.
The Master of Great Virtue Wenyuan asked, "Does the Chan Master know the place where he will be reborn? The Master said, "I have not yet died; why discuss being born?
To know birth is itself the dharma of non-birth (*anutpāda*). There is no dharma apart from birth that can be called non-birth. The Patriarch said:

"When arising, it is precisely non-arising. [The student] asked: "Can those who have not yet seen their nature also attain this? The Master said: "It is because they themselves have not seen their nature;
it is not that they lack nature. Why is this? Seeing is itself nature; if there were no nature, one could not see.

Cognition is itself nature, therefore it is called 'the nature of cognition. Clarity is itself nature, therefore it is called 'the nature of clarity. That which can give rise to the myriad dharmas is called 'dharmas.'"
Nature is also called the Dharma-body. The Patriarch Aśvaghoṣa said: "That which is called 'Dharma' refers to the mind of sentient beings.
If the mind arises, all dharmas arise; if the mind does not arise, dharmas have no source from which to arise, nor do they have names.
Those who are deluded do not know that the Dharma-body has no form, yet manifests forms in response to things; consequently, they claim that every verdant bamboo shoot is entirely the Dharma-body.
The lush yellow flowers are nothing other than *prajñā*. If the yellow flowers were *prajñā*, then *prajñā* would be identical to insentient things.

If the green bamboos were the *dharmakāya*, then the *dharmakāya* would be identical to grass and trees. If this were so, a person eating bamboo shoots would be eating the *dharmakāya* in its entirety.
How can such words be worthy of being recorded? To face the Buddha and yet be deluded, seeking him for long kalpas—this is the total [delusion].
Within the Dharma, people are deluded and seek it externally. Therefore, for one who understands the Way, walking, standing, sitting, and reclining are none other than the Way;
for one who has awakened to the Dharma, moving freely in all directions is none other than the Dharma.
The Venerable One asked again: "Can the great void give rise to spiritual wisdom? Does the true mind engage with good and evil? Is a person possessed of greed and desire on the Way?
Will a person who clings to right and wrong eventually attain mental penetration? Does a person who gives rise to thoughts upon encountering objects possess meditative concentration?
Does a person dwelling in stillness and silence possess wisdom? Does a person harboring arrogance toward things possess a sense of self? [What of one who] clings to emptiness?"
"Is there a person who possesses wisdom? Is it one who seeks proof by searching through texts; one who seeks the Buddha through ascetic practices;

one who seeks the Buddha apart from the mind; or one who clings to the mind as being the Buddha? Are all these considered to be following the Way? I beg the Chan Master to explain each of these points. The Master said:

The great void does not give birth to spiritual wisdom; the true mind does not depend upon good or evil. Those whose cravings and desires are deep have shallow faculties; those who contend over right and wrong have not yet attained penetration.
Those who give rise to thoughts upon encountering objects lack stability; those who dwell in silence and forget their artifice have sunk into dullness.

Those who are arrogant toward things and hold themselves in high esteem are strong in egoism; those who cling to emptiness or cling to existence are all deluded. Those who seek proof by following the words become increasingly obstructed.
Those who seek the Buddha through asceticism are all deluded; those who seek the Buddha apart from the mind are non-Buddhists; those who cling to the mind as being the Buddha are possessed by Māra.
The Venerable One said, "If it is so, then there must ultimately be nothing at all. The Master said, "Ultimately, O Venerable One, is this [the case]."
"It is not that they are ultimately non-existent. The Venerable One, leaping for joy, prostrated in thanks and departed.
The Master ascended the hall and said: "All of you are fortunately already good 'men of no affairs. Why do you toil so hard to create [karmic causes] only to take up the cangue and fall into prison?
Day after day until nightfall you rush about, saying, 'I am practicing Chan, I am studying the Way, I understand the Buddha-dharma.'"
In this way, there is no turning back and no meeting [with the truth]. It is merely running after sounds and forms; when will there ever be a time of rest? I have heard the Master of Jiangxi say:
"Your own precious treasury is fully complete with everything; its use is at your own disposal, requiring no seeking from without.
From this moment on, I shall cease for a time and enjoy my own wealth according to my needs—this may truly be called blissful.

Alive! There is not a single dharma to be grasped, nor a single dharma to be discarded. One does not perceive the marks of arising and ceasing in any dharma, nor the marks of coming and going in any dharma.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is not even a speck of dust that is not one's own wealth and treasure.
Simply observe with meticulous care: the single essence of the Three Jewels is constantly manifest within your own mind.
There is no need for doubt or anxiety; do not engage in discursive thought, and do not seek or search for it. The nature of the mind is primordially pure. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"All phenomena are neither born nor extinguished. If one can understand them in this way, the Buddhas are always present before one. Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* states:

The Sūtra says: "Contemplate the true mark of the body; contemplate the Buddha in the same way. If you do not let your thoughts stir in response to sounds and forms, and do not give rise to understanding by pursuing appearances, you will naturally proceed without affairs. Do not stand for long. Take care.
On this day, the great assembly gathered together and remained for a long time without dispersing. The Master said, "Why do you all remain here and not leave?
I have already presented my response to you; will you now consent to cease? What is there to doubt? Do not misapply your efforts."
It is a waste of effort and breath. If you have any doubts, feel free to ask as much as you wish at once.
At that time, a monk named Fayuan asked: "What is the Buddha? What is the Dharma? What is the Sangha? What is the Three Jewels of One Substance?
I pray that the Master will grant us instruction. The Master said: "The mind is the Buddha; there is no need to seek the Buddha by means of the Buddha. The mind is..."
The Dharma: one does not seek the Dharma by means of the Dharma; the Buddha-dharma is non-dual. When these are in harmony, they constitute the Sangha;

thus, they are the Three Jewels as a single essence. As the Sūtra says: "Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. When body, speech, and mind are pure, it is called the appearance of a Buddha in the world;
when the three karmas are impure, it is called the parinirvāṇa of a Buddha. It is like there being no joy at the time of anger. Joy...

At that time, there is no anger; it is but a single mind, truly without dual substance. This is the natural state (*dharmatā*) of primordial wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), wherein the untainted (*anāsrava*) manifests before one.
It is like a snake transforming into a dragon without changing its scales, or sentient beings turning their minds toward Buddhahood without changing their countenances.

Nature is fundamentally pure and does not depend on cultivation for its completion. To have a realization or a cultivation [as if they were newly acquired] is to be like one who possesses overweening pride (*adhimāna*). In true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), there is no obstruction.
Its application is inexhaustible; it is without beginning and without end. For those of sharp faculties who attain sudden enlightenment, its function is peerless—this is *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
That the mind has no form or appearance is the subtle and wondrous body of form (*rūpakāya*). That which is signless is the true reality (*dharmatā*).
That the nature and characteristics of the *dharmakāya* are essentially empty is the boundless body of space. That it is adorned with the myriad practices is the dharma of merit.

Body. This Dharma-body is the root of all transformations. It receives various names according to the circumstances: because its wisdom and function are inexhaustible, it is called the "Inexhaustible Treasury";
because it can give rise to all phenomena, it is called the "Fundamental Dharma-treasury"; because it possesses all-knowledge, it is the "Wisdom-treasury";

and because all phenomena return to Suchness, it is called the "Tathāgata-treasury. As the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata is the meaning of the Suchness of all phenomena. Furthermore, it says: "The World..."
"Among all phenomena that arise and perish, there is not a single dharma that does not return to Suchness.
A visitor asked, "Your disciple does not yet know which is most excellent: the Vinaya Master, the Dharma Master, or the Chan Master.

I pray that the Honored One will compassionately instruct me. The Master said, "Now, as for the Vinaya Master, he opens the Dharma-treasury of the *Vinaya* and transmits the longevity [of the teachings]."

This is the lingering influence of that tradition. He thoroughly mastered the precepts regarding transgressions and their maintenance, as well as the principles of opening and closing [the path]. Upholding the majestic deportment, he established models for conduct.

By reciting the three rounds of the *karmavācanā*, he acted as the primary cause for attaining the four fruits of the path. Were it not for one of long-standing virtue with white eyebrows, who would dare to act so precipitously?
As for the Dharma Master, seated upon the lion’s throne, he poured forth the eloquence of a cascading river; before a vast assembly of people, he opened the profound gateway to the mysteries.
It opens the wondrous gate of Prajñā and bestows the three wheels of giving equally within emptiness. Were it not for a dragon or an elephant treading upon it, who would dare to face this?

As for the Chan master, he grasps the essential pivot and directly realizes the source of the mind; appearing and disappearing, rolling up and unfolding, he responds to things with total freedom and mastery.
When one thoroughly harmonizes phenomena and principle, one suddenly beholds the Tathāgata, uproots the deep roots of birth and death, and attains the samādhi of direct manifestation.

If one does not settle into dhyāna and śamatha, one will be utterly bewildered upon reaching this point. The Dharma is bestowed according to individual capacity; although the three studies differ, when the meaning is grasped, the words are forgotten.
How could the One Vehicle be otherwise? Thus the Sūtra says: "In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the teaching of the One Vehicle."
"There is neither two nor three; it is only through the Buddha’s skillful means that he speaks. He merely uses provisional names to guide sentient beings.

The guest said, "Master, you have profoundly penetrated the intent of the Buddha and possess unimpeded eloquence. He asked again, "Are the three teachings of Confucianism, Daoism, and Buddhism the same or different?
The Master replied, "For those of great capacity, they are the same when applied; for those of limited faculties, they are different when clung to. In total...

Function arises from the single nature; yet, due to differences in the capacities and perspectives of sentient beings, it manifests as three. Delusion and enlightenment depend on the person, not on whether the teachings differ or agree.
When the Venerable Master Daoguang of the Weishi (Vijñaptimātra) school asked, "With what mind does the Chan Master cultivate the Way? the Master replied, "I, the old monk..."

"There is no mind that can be employed; there is no Way that can be cultivated. [The student] asked, "If there is no mind that can be employed and no Way that can be cultivated, why do you gather the assembly every day to exhort people to study Chan and cultivate the Way? The Master said, "This old monk does not even have enough ground to stick a锥 (a small awl) into."
"Why have you gathered a crowd here? "The old monk has no tongue; when have I ever encouraged people to come?
"You are lying to my face, Master," he said. The Master replied, "If even this old monk has no tongue to encourage others, how could I possibly speak falsely?
"I still do not understand the Master's discourse," he said. The Master replied, "I myself do not understand it either."
The Preceptor Zhi of Jianghuayan asked, "Why do you not allow that every verdant bamboo shoot is the Dharmakāya, and that every lush yellow flower is nothing other than Prajñā?
The Master said, "The Dharmakāya has no form; it takes shape by responding to the green bamboo. Prajñā has no cognition;
it manifests its appearance in contrast to the yellow flowers. It is not that there is Prajñā and the Dharmakāya apart from those yellow flowers and green bamboo."
"It is the body. Therefore, a sutra says: 'The Buddha’s true Dharma-body is like empty space; it manifests forms in response to things, like the moon reflected in water.
If the yellow flowers were Prajñā, then Prajñā would be the same as insentient matter. If the green bamboo were the Dharmakāya, then the green bamboo would still be able to function and respond.
Master, do you understand? The student replied, "I do not comprehend this meaning. The Master said, "If one has seen one's nature..."
To say "the Way is" is acceptable; to say "the Way is not" is also acceptable. One speaks according to function without being obstructed by right or wrong.

For those who have not seen their nature, when they speak of green bamboos, they are attached to the green bamboos; when they speak of yellow flowers, they are attached to the yellow flowers; when they speak of the Dharma-body, they are obstructed by the Dharma-body.
When it was said that they did not recognize Prajñā while speaking of Prajñā, everyone became embroiled in contentious debate. Zhizhe bowed in apology and departed.
Someone asked him, "If one practices with the mind, how long will it take to attain liberation? The Master replied, "To practice with the mind is like trying to wash away dirt with slippery mud.
Prajñā is profound and subtle; it is fundamentally unborn from the beginning. When its great function manifests, it does not depend on time or season. He said:

"Can ordinary people also attain this? The Master said, "One who has realized their nature is no longer an ordinary person. Those who suddenly awaken to the Supreme Vehicle transcend both the ordinary and the holy.
For the deluded, there is talk of ordinary and holy; for the awakened, they transcend both birth-and-death and nirvana. The deluded speak of phenomena and principles;
the awakened possess the great function that is boundless in its application. The deluded seek attainment and realization; the awakened have nothing to attain."
There is no seeking. Those who delude themselves expect realization after distant kalpas;
those who awaken see it suddenly. The Master Weimo asked: The Sūtra says, "Those six heterodox teachers are your teachers;
because you left home under them, where those teachers have fallen, you too shall fall. Those who give to you are not called fields of merit; they provide for you [in vain]."

Such persons fall into the three evil realms; they slander the Buddha and destroy the Dharma. They do not enter the ranks of the assembly and shall never attain nirvana. If you are like this, then you may take this food.
Now, I request that the Meditation Master clearly explain liberation for me. The Master said:

"Those who are deludedly devoted to the six sense organs are called the Six Teachers. To seek the Buddha outside the mind is to be known as a non-Buddhist (tīrthika). If there were any substance to be given away,"
One is not called a field of merit. To give rise to a mind that accepts offerings is to fall into the three evil realms.
If you can slander the Buddha, this is not seeking the Buddha. If you destroy the Dharma, this is not seeking the Dharma. If you do not enter the ranks of the Sangha, this is not seeking the Sangha.
If you ultimately do not attain extinction, the function of wisdom manifests before you. If there is such an understanding, then...
One attains the food of the joy of Dharma and the delight of dhyāna.
There was a practitioner who asked: "If someone asks the Buddha, the Buddha answers; if they ask about the Dharma, he answers about the Dharma. This is called the 'Dharma-gate of a Single Word.'"
"I do not know whether this is so," [the questioner] said. The Master replied, "It is like a parrot learning human speech; it cannot speak for itself because it lacks wisdom.
Therefore, it is like using water to wash water, or using fire to burn fire—it is utterly devoid of purpose."
Someone asked, "Are 'yan' (speech) and 'yu' (discourse) the same or different? The Master said, "They are one and the same. When speech forms a sentence, it is called discourse.

For instance, when brilliant eloquence flows forth like the waters of a great river, and sharp wit unfolds in succession like pearls pouring from a rounded vessel—thus encompassing the myriad phenomena and known as a 'suspended river' that cleaves the ocean of meaning—this is discourse. As for speech..."

This single character expresses the mind: internally it abides in the profound and subtle, while externally it manifests wondrous signs. Though disturbed by ten thousand occasions, it is not disordered;
though turbid and clear elements mingle, they are always distinguished. Even King Qi felt ashamed of the words of the Great Officer, and Mañjuśrī still marveled at the discourse of Vimalakīrti.
How then can ordinary people of today understand it?
Master Yuan asked, "Chan Master, you constantly say that 'this very mind is Buddha. That is impossible.

Furthermore, a Bodhisattva on the first bhūmi manifests bodies throughout a hundred Buddha-worlds, increasing tenfold at each successive stage. Chan Master, try to manifest some supernatural power for me to see."

The Master asked, "Upādhyāya, are you yourself an ordinary person or a sage? He replied, "I am an ordinary person. The Master said, "Since you are an ordinary monk yet can inquire about such a realm, it is as the Sūtra says:
'O worthy one, your mind has highs and lows; it does not rely upon the Buddha-wisdom. This is precisely what that means.
He asked again, "Every time you, Meditation Master, say that if the realization of the Way manifests before one, the body is immediately liberated, that is not correct."
The Master asked, "Suppose there is a person who has practiced goodness throughout their entire life, yet suddenly finds themselves with stolen goods in their hands;
are they a thief in that very moment? The monk replied, "I know for certain that they are. The Master said, "If you can now see this clearly, why is it that you have not attained liberation?
The monk replied, "It is simply impossible right now; one must pass through three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas before it can be achieved. The Master said, "As for those *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas..."
"Is there anything more to say? Yuan raised his voice and said, "Can it be logically justified to compare a thief with liberation?
The Master said, "Ācārya, you yourself do not understand the Way; you must not obstruct others from understanding it. Your own eyes are not open, yet you resent everyone else for seeing things.
Yuan flushed with anger and departed, saying, "Though old, you are utterly devoid of the Way. The Master remarked, "As for that one who has just left..."
"This is your path.
When the lecture master of Zhi-guan-hui asked, "Can a Chan master discern demons? the Master replied, "To give rise to a thought is the celestial demon;
not to give rise to a thought is the aggregate demon; whether thoughts arise or do not arise is the affliction demon. Within my True Dharma, there is none such as these."
Regarding this matter, [the student] asked, "What is the meaning of the 'three contemplations within one mind'?

The Master said, "The past mind has already passed away; the future mind has not yet arrived; the present mind dwells nowhere. Within this interval, what further mind could you employ to give rise to contemplation?

The student said, "Chan Master, you do not understand *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). The Master asked, "Does the Master of the Tripitaka understand them? He replied, "I understand. The Master said, "As for the Great Master Zhiyi..."

The Master says that explaining the cessation of stillness (*śamatha*) destroys stillness; explaining the contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) destroys contemplation. Abiding in stillness causes one to sink into birth and death; abiding in contemplation causes the mind to become distracted.
Should one direct the mind toward stillness? Or should one arouse the mind toward contemplation? If there is a mind engaged in contemplation, this is the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).

If there is no mind engaged in contemplation, this is the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). To hold both "existence" and "non-existence" constitutes the duality of views. I request you, O Master of the Assembly, to examine this in detail.
"Tell me," [the monk] said. The Master replied, "If you ask in such a manner, neither can be spoken. The Master asked, "When did you ever practice *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight)?
Someone asked, "Is *prajñā* (wisdom) great? The Master said, "It is great. [The monk] asked, "How great is it? The Master said, "It has no boundaries. [The monk] asked, "Is *prajñā* small?
The Master said, "It is small. [The monk] asked, "How small is it? The Master said, "It cannot be seen. [The monk] asked, "Where is it? The Master said—
[The student] asked, "Where is it not so?
Weimo (Vimalakīrti) the Seat-Master asked, "The Sutra says that the various Bodhisattvas each entered the Dharma-gate of non-duality. Is Vimalakīrti’s silence the ultimate [realization]?
The Master said, "It is not yet the ultimate. If the Sage’s intent were exhausted there, what would he have further explained in the third fascicle?"
The Master [of the Dharma-seat] remained silent for a long while and said, "I request the Chan Master to explain the meaning of what has not yet reached ultimate completion.
The Master replied, "In the first fascicle of the sutra, the assembly is addressed and the ten great disciples are called upon to dwell in the mind.
In the second fascicle, each of the bodhisattvas speaks of entering the gate of non-duality, using words to manifest the wordless. Mañjuśrī then uses the wordless to manifest the wordless."
Vimalakīrti employs neither speech nor silence; thus, he remains silent, thereby withdrawing his previous words.
In the third fascicle, the teaching arises from this silence, further manifesting the operation of supernatural powers. "Do you understand, Master of the Seat? He replied, "How extraordinary!"
The Master said, "It is not yet like this. [The student] asked, "For what reason is it not yet so? The Master said, "I have spoken thus merely to shatter people's attachments and deluded sentiments.

According to the intent of the scriptures, they speak only of the emptiness and stillness of form and mind, so as to cause one to see one's original nature; they teach the abandonment of false practices and the entry into true practice.
Do not seek meaning through words, paper, or ink; simply understand the two characters 'Pure Name' (Vimalakīrti) and you will be done."
It is attained. "Purity" (jing) is the fundamental essence (ben-ti); "name" (ming) is the phenomenal function (ji-yong). From the fundamental essence, the phenomenal function arises;

from the phenomenal function, one returns to the fundamental essence. Essence and function are not two; the fundamental and the phenomenal are not distinct. Thus, the ancients said: "Although the fundamental and the phenomenal are distinct..."

The inconceivable is one, yet even this "one" is not one. If one recognizes that the two characters "Pure Name" (Vimalakīrti) are merely provisional designations, what more need be said of ultimate or non-ultimate?
There is no before or after; it is neither beginning nor end; it is neither pure nor name.
It simply reveals the inconceivable liberation of the original nature of sentient beings. Those who do not perceive this nature will never see this throughout their entire lives.

Li asked: "If all phenomena are entirely empty and the nature of consciousness is likewise—just like a bubble of water that, once dispersed, never reunites, and once the body dies, is never born again—then it is simply empty and non-existent.
Where, then, could there still be a nature of consciousness? The Master said: "A bubble is caused by..."
"Water exists. When the bubbles disperse, the water itself is not immediately gone. The body arises because of its nature; when the body dies, how can one say that the nature is extinguished?
The monk said, "Since you say there is a nature, bring it out for me to see. The Master said, "Do you believe that tomorrow morning exists? He replied, "I believe it does.
The Master said, "Then I shall bring tomorrow morning here for you to see. The monk said, "Tomorrow morning truly exists, but it cannot be obtained right now. The Master said, "Tomorrow morning..."
It cannot be said that it is unattainable, nor can it be said that there is no tomorrow; it is simply that you do not perceive your own nature.

It cannot be said that there is no nature, for right now you see yourself putting on clothes, eating, walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, yet you fail to recognize it face-to-face—this may truly be called ignorance and delusion.
If you wish to see tomorrow, it is no different from today; to seek nature by means of nature will lead you to never seeing it, even after ten thousand kalpas. It is like a person who...
[The Master] saw the sun; it was not that there was no sun.
A Dharma Master lecturing on the *Qinglong shu* asked, "The Sūtra says, 'There is no dharma that can be preached; this is called preaching the Dharma.
How do you, Chan Master, realize this? The Master replied, "Because the essence of Prajñā is ultimately pure and tranquil, there is not a single thing that can be apprehended. This is it.
It is called the "non-dharma. Within the essence of the emptiness and stillness of *prajñā*, it possesses functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
thus, there is nothing it does not know. This is what is meant by "preaching the Dharma. Therefore, it is said: "There is no dharma that can be preached; this is what is called preaching the Dharma."
A presiding master of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra asked, "Chan Master, do you believe that insentient things are Buddhas? The Master replied, "I do not believe it.
If insentient things were Buddhas, then living people would be inferior to the dead; even dead donkeys and dead dogs would be superior to living people.
He continued, "The Sūtra says: 'The Buddha-body is the Dharma-body. It is born from precepts, concentration, and wisdom; it arises from the three clarities and the six supernormal powers.'"
[He] was born from all wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*). If one says that insentient things are the Buddha, then, Venerable Sir, you should become a Buddha this very moment upon your death.
A Dharma Master asked: "The merit of upholding the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is the greatest; do you, Master, believe this? The Master replied: "I do not believe it."

[The opponent] said: "If that were so, the more than ten volumes of *Lingyan zhuan* (Accounts of Spiritual Efficacy) would all be unworthy of belief. The Master said: "When living people maintain filial piety, there is naturally a corresponding response (*yinggan*).
It is not that the white bones themselves can possess such a response. The sutras are merely words, paper, and ink;

since the nature of words, paper, and ink is empty (*śūnya*), where could spiritual efficacy reside? Spiritual efficacy lies in the person upholding the sutra applying their mind [to it]. Therefore..."
"Supernatural powers move things. Try placing a single scroll of scripture upon a table; even if no one upholds it, can it not manifest its own spiritual efficacy?
A monk asked: "I do not yet understand how all names and characteristics, as well as the characteristics of dharmas—whether in speech or in silence—are to be comprehended and harmonized."
"There is no before or after. The Master said: "When a single thought arises, it is fundamentally without form and without name. How can one speak of before and after?

Failing to realize that names and forms are fundamentally pure, one falsely calculates that there is before and after. Now, names and forms are like a lock; it cannot be opened except by the key of wisdom.
Those who dwell in the Middle Way find their ailment in the Middle Way; those who dwell in the two extremes find their ailment in the two extremes. Not...

To know that present functioning is the peerless *dharmakāya*, yet to remain deluded regarding awakening and to lose sight of the nature of ordinary beings, is to give rise to birth and death oneself and thereby bury true wisdom.
Whether one seeks to sever afflictions or strives for bodhi, one turns one's back on *prajñā*.
Someone asked, "Reverend Master, why do you not believe in Chan? The Master replied, "The principle is profound and difficult to manifest; names and forms are easy to grasp.
It is for this reason that those who have not seen their nature do not believe. One who has seen their nature is called a Buddha; only one who recognizes the Buddha can truly enter the faith.
The Buddha is not distant from people, but people are distant from the Buddha. The Buddha is created by the mind; deluded people turn instead toward words and letters."
Seek within. Those who have awakened perceive by turning toward their own minds; those who are deluded cultivate causes while awaiting results. Those who have awakened realize the mind is signless;

those who are deluded cling to objects and guard the self as "mine. For those who have awakened, the application of *prajñā* is manifest before them; for fools, they cling to emptiness or existence and remain stagnant.
The wise see into their nature and understand all signs with spiritual penetration. Those of dry wisdom and mere eloquence exhaust themselves verbally; the one of great wisdom...

When one realizes the essence, the mind is at ease. A Bodhisattva illuminates everything upon contact with objects, whereas a Śrāvaka’s mind is obscured by fear of external circumstances. To the awakened, daily life is non-arising;
to the deluded, what lies before them is separated from the Buddha.
A person asked, "How can one attain supernatural powers (ṛddhi)? The Master said, "The nature of spirit is numinous and penetrating; it pervades the entire dharma-realm.
Mountains, rivers, stones, and walls cannot obstruct its coming and going; in a single kṣaṇa, it travels ten thousand li with no trace left behind. Fire cannot burn it, and water cannot drown it.
It is only because ignorant people lack wisdom and mind that they desire to fly through the air using the four great elements. As the Sūtra says: 'Ordinary worldlings grasp at appearances.'"
I teach according to what is appropriate. That the mind has no form or appearance is itself the subtle and wondrous form-body (*rūpakāya*).

The signless is the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*). Since the essence of the true mark is emptiness, it is called the boundless space-body. Because it is adorned with the myriad practices, it is called the merit-dharma-body (*guṇadharmakāya*).
This very dharma-body is the source of the myriad practices; names are established according to its functions. To speak of the reality, it is simply this.
It is the pure *dharmakāya*.
Someone asked, "If one cultivates the Way with a single mind, can past karmic obstructions be extinguished? The Master said, "For those who have not seen their nature, they cannot be extinguished.
For those who have seen their nature, it is like the sun shining upon frost and snow. Furthermore, for those who have seen their nature, it is like a pile of... [snow].
Grass and other vegetation compared to Mount Sumeru: using but a single spark of fire. Karmic obstructions are like the grass; wisdom is like the fire. [A questioner] asks:

"How can one know that karmic obstructions have been exhausted? The Master says: "When the mind of the present perceives the events of past and future lives as if seeing them face-to-face, and when the Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the future, and all phenomena, are simultaneous—this is what the sutra means when it says: 'To know all dharmas in a single thought-moment is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).'"
Because of the accomplishment of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
A practitioner asked: "How can one abide in the True Dharma? The Master said: "To seek to abide in the True Dharma is itself erroneous.
Why? Because the Dharma has neither error nor correctness. [The practitioner] asked: "How then can one become a Buddha and depart? The Master said: "It is not by abandoning the multitude."
"Give rise to the mind, but do not defile its self-nature. As the Sūtra says: "The mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.
[The student] asked: "If one understands it in this way, will one attain liberation? The Master said: "It is fundamentally unbound; there is no need to seek liberation."
The Dharma transcends words and letters; it is not to be sought within a few phrases. The Dharma is not of the past, present, or future;
it cannot be realized through cause and effect. The Dharma transcends all things and is beyond comparison. The Dharmakāya is formless, yet it manifests forms in response to objects.
One does not seek liberation by departing from the mundane world.
A monk asked, "What is *prajñā*? The Master said, "If you suspect that something is not it, try explaining why. The monk asked again, "How does one realize one's nature (*xing*)?
The Master said, "Seeing is itself the nature; without the nature, there can be no seeing. The monk asked again, "What is cultivation (*xiūxíng*)?
The Master said, "Simply do not defile your own nature—that is cultivation. Do not deceive yourself—that is it."
"Practice. When the Great Function manifests before you, that is the Peerless Dharma-body. He asked again, "Is there evil within this nature?
The Master said, "Within this, even 'good' is not established. He asked, "If neither good nor evil is established, where will one employ the mind?
The Master said, "To employ the mind by means of the mind is a great perversion. He asked, "What then is it? The Master said, "There is nothing to do."
[The Master] said: "Birth is likewise not something that can be affirmed.
When someone asked, "If a person is traveling by boat and the bottom of the boat pierces and kills snails and clams, does this person receive the retribution for the sin, or does the boat receive it?
The Master said: "Both the person and the boat are without intention; the sin lies precisely with you. It is like a raging wind that breaks trees and causes damage."
Life has no agent and no recipient. Within the world, there is nowhere that is not a place where sentient beings undergo suffering.

A monk asked: "I do not yet understand how the momentum of emotional attachment, the momentum of pointing to objects, the momentum of speech and silence, and even the momentum of raising an eyebrow or moving an eye—how can these all be comprehended within a single thought-moment?
The Master said: "There are no phenomena external to nature; it is for those who employ this subtlety."
Movement and stillness are both wondrous. For one whose mind is true, speech and silence are both true; for one who has realized the Way, walking, standing, sitting, and lying down are the Way.
Yet, because people are deluded regarding their own nature, the myriad afflictions arise. He asked again: "What is the fundamental principle of the Dharma? The Master said:
"According to how it is established, there are manifold meanings. Mañjuśrī established all dharmas upon the groundless foundation. [The student] said: "Do not be like that."

"Is it not the same as the great void? The Master said, "Are you afraid it is the same as the great void? He replied, "I am afraid. The Master said, "One who understands fear is not the same as the great void.
He asked again, "How can one understand that which words cannot reach? The Master said, "Right now, at the very moment you are speaking."

He asked, "In what way could there be anything that does not reach [the Dharma]? Some ten or more virtuous elders asked the same question together. He cited a sutra which says: "They will destroy the Buddha-Dharma. They asked, "We do not yet know whether the Buddha-Dharma can indeed be destroyed.
The Master said, "Ordinary people and non-Buddhists claim the Buddha-Dharma can be destroyed; those of the Two Vehicles claim it cannot."
"Ruinous! Within my True Dharma, these two views do not exist. If one speaks of the True Dharma, it is not only ordinary people and non-Buddhists;
even those of the Two Vehicles who have not yet reached the stage of Buddhahood are likewise considered evil persons. He asked again:

"Do the True Dharma, the illusory Dharma, the empty Dharma, and the non-empty Dharma each possess their own seed-nature (*gotra*)? The Master said: "Although the Dharma has no seed-nature, it manifests in accordance with all things. It is the mind..."
Illusion is such that all things are illusory; if there were even a single dharma that were not illusory, then illusion would possess a fixed nature.
The mind is empty such that all things are empty; if there were even a single dharma that were not empty, the meaning of emptiness could not be established. When deluded, people pursue dharmas.

When awakening occurs, the Dharma depends upon the person. Just as the myriad phenomena of the universe reach their ultimate limit in space, and the hundred rivers and various streams reach their ultimate limit in the ocean, so too do all sages and worthies reach their ultimate limit in the Buddha.
The twelve divisions of the scriptures, the five sections of the Vinaya, and the five Vedas reach their ultimate limit in the mind.
The mind is the wondrous root of total retention (*dhāraṇī*) and the great source of the myriad dharmas. It is also...
It is named the Great Treasury of Wisdom and Unabiding Nirvana; these hundreds of thousands of names are merely different designations according to one's state of mind.
He asked again, "What is illusion? The Master said, "Illusion has no fixed form; it is like a whirling firebrand, like a city of the Gandharvas."
They are like mechanical wooden figures, like a mirage, like flowers in the sky; none of them possess any substantial reality. Again he asked, "What is called the 'Great Illusionist'?
The Master said, "The mind is called the Great Illusionist. The body is the great illusory city. Names and appearances are the great illusory food and clothing.

Throughout the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is no phenomenon outside of illusion. Yet ordinary people do not recognize this illusion; everywhere they are deluded by illusory karma."
The Śrāvakas fear illusory phenomena; they enter into quiescence with their minds obscured. The Bodhisattvas recognize illusory dharmas and penetrate the essence of illusion;

they are not bound by any names or characteristics. The Buddha is the Great Master of Illusion; he turns the Great Dharma-wheel of illusion, achieves the Great Nirvāṇa of illusion, and transforms illusory arising and ceasing into non-arising and non-ceasing.
He transforms lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges that are defiled into the pure Dharma-realm.

A monk asked, "For what reason do you not permit the recitation of sutras, calling it 'the speech of a guest'? The Master said, "It is like a parrot that merely mimics human speech but does not grasp the meaning of people.

[The student] said, "That is why you do not permit it. [The Master asked,] "Do you mean that there is a separate meaning apart from words and language?

The Master said, "Your speaking in this way is merely repeating what others have said. [The student] said, "Since both are equally language, why do you specifically disallow this? The Master said, "Listen closely now. The scriptures have clear evidence for this.
What I speak is the language of meaning (*artha-vākya*), not the language of letters (*vyañjana-vākya*); what sentient beings speak is the language of letters, not the language of meaning."

Regarding meaning: one who grasps the meaning transcends empty words; one who awakens to the principle surpasses written characters. Since the Dharma transcends language and writing, how can it be sought within a few sentences?
Therefore, those who give rise to bodhicitta grasp the meaning and forget the words; they awaken to the principle and set aside the teachings.
This is just like catching the fish and forgetting the trap, or catching the rabbit and forgetting the snare.

He asked again, "Does the Buddha-dharma reside within the three temporal limits? The Master said, "Its manifestation is without marks, so it does not exist outside them;
its application is inexhaustible, so it does not exist inside them. There is no place of abiding in between; thus, the three temporal limits cannot contain it."
[The student] said, "I have attained it. The Master said, "These words are utterly confused. The student asked, "When you say the word 'confused,' does it reside within or without?
[The student] replied, "Upon my investigation, there is no trace of it, either within or without. The Master said, "If there is no trace, then it is clear that what was said before was not confused.
[The student] asked, "How then can one become a Buddha? The Master said, "This mind is the Buddha; this mind creates the Buddha. [The student] asked, "..."
"When sentient beings enter hell, does their Buddha-nature also enter? The Master said, "At this very moment when one is committing evil, is there still any goodness?
[The monk] said, "No. The Master said, "When sentient beings enter hell, it is the same with their Buddha-nature. [The monk] asked, "If all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, how is this so?
The Master said, "When it functions as a Buddha, it is Buddha-nature; when it functions as a thief, it is thief-nature."
To act for the benefit of sentient beings is the nature of sentient beings. This nature has no form or appearance; names are established according to its functions. As a sutra says:
"All worthy and holy ones are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)."
A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "Apart from the mind, there is no Buddha. The monk asked, "What is the Dharma-body? The Master said, "The mind is the Dharma-body;
because it can give rise to the myriad dharmas, it is called the body of the Dharma-realm. The *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* says:
"That which is called 'Dharma' refers to the mind of sentient beings. It is based upon this mind that the Mahāyāna is revealed."
Meaning. Again, he asked: "What is meant by 'there is a great scripture within a single minute particle'? The Master replied: "Wisdom is the scripture. A sutra says:
"There is a great scripture, equal in measure to the three thousandfold world system, contained within a single minute particle.

A "particle" refers to the particle of the mind of a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*). Therefore, it is said that from within the dust of a single thought-moment, one expounds as many teachings as there are sands in the Ganges.
Verse: Those of the time do not recognize it themselves. He asked again: "What is called the City of Great Meaning?
What is called the King of Great Meaning? The Master said: "The body is the City of Great Meaning; the mind is the King of Great Meaning. As the Sūtra says:

"Those who have heard much are skilled in meaning, not in verbal expression. Verbal expression arises and perishes, while meaning neither arises nor perishes. Meaning has no form or appearance; it resides within verbal expression."
Externally, the body is the great scripture, and the mind is the great King of Meaning. If one does not clearly recognize the mind, it cannot be called "skillful in meaning";

such a person is merely one who studies words. He asked again: The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that the nine classes of sentient beings are all delivered and enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, yet it also says that in reality there are no sentient beings who attain deliverance. Regarding these two passages of the sutra...

"How can one harmonize and understand the preceding and following passages? A person asked. "Everyone says that while one truly delivers sentient beings, one does not grasp at the mark of a sentient being.
I have always harbored this doubt and cannot resolve it; I beg the Master to explain it for me. The Master said: "The nine classes of sentient beings are fully present within a single body;
they are formed as one acts. Therefore, ignorance constitutes egg-birth; being enveloped by afflictions constitutes womb-birth; and being soaked in the waters of craving..."
Moisture-born beings arise through humidity; those who suddenly give rise to afflictions are transformation-born. Awakening is itself Buddhahood; delusion is termed "sentient beings.
A Bodhisattva regards every thought-moment as a sentient being; if one realizes that the essence of every thought-moment is entirely empty, this is called "delivering sentient beings.
The wise deliver those not yet formed within their own fundamental limit; since that which is not yet formed is empty, they know it as such.
"In truth, there is no sentient being who attains liberation.
A monk asked, "Are words the mind? The Master said, "Words are conditions; they are not the mind. The monk asked, "Apart from conditions, what is the mind?
The Master said, "Apart from words, there is no mind. The monk said, "If there is no mind apart from words, how can it be so?"

[The student asked about] the mind. The Master said: "The mind has no form or appearance; it is not apart from language, nor is it not apart from language. The mind is eternally serene, its application being ever-sovereign.
As the Patriarch said: "If one realizes that the mind is no-mind, only then does one understand the dharma of mind and mind."

A monk asked, "What is the equal cultivation of concentration and wisdom? The Master said, "Concentration is the essence; wisdom is the function. Wisdom arises from concentration, and concentration is returned to through wisdom.
They are like water and its waves—of one substance, with no priority or sequence. This is called the equal cultivation of concentration and wisdom."
Now, those who have left the household life must not seek after words or pursue phrases; walking, standing, sitting, and lying down are all the functioning of your own nature.
Where, then, would they not be in accord with the Way? For now, simply rest for a while. If you do not follow the winds of external objects, [the mind will naturally settle].
The nature of water is eternally clear and still. Be careful in the midst of no affairs.
This concludes the first volume of the *Recorded Sayings* (Yulu) of the disciples from all quarters who visited for instruction.
Attached herein is the First Patriarch, Great Master Bodhidharma’s Dharma Gate of Settling the Mind.
(From the *Lian Deng Hui Yao*):
In delusion, the person pursues phenomena; in awakening, phenomena pursue the person. In awakening, consciousness subsumes form; in delusion, form subsumes consciousness.
Whatever is conceptualized, calculated, or discriminated by the mind—all that which is the manifestation of one’s own mind—is entirely a dream.

If consciousness and the mind are stilled and extinguished, such that there is no locus for any thought, this is called perfect awakening. Question: What is meant by "the manifestation of one’s own mind"? Answer:

When one perceives all phenomena as existing, their existence does not arise from itself; it is constructed as existent by the calculations of one’s own mind. When one perceives all phenomena as non-existent, their non-existence does not arise from itself... [The text continues with the same structure regarding the non-existence of phenomena].
There is nothing. One’s own mind calculates it as non-existent, and so it is with all phenomena;

they are all calculated by one's own mind as existent or non-existent. Furthermore, if a person has committed all manner of transgressions, upon seeing the Dharma-King within themselves, they immediately attain liberation.
If one attains liberation through the activity, their strength is robust; if one sees the Dharma within the activity, then...
In every place, one does not lose mindfulness. Those who seek understanding through words and letters have weak power; those who engage directly with phenomena and reality are profound.

Whether you perform various activities, leap about, or stumble, none of it transcends the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). If one were to enter the dharma-realm by means of the dharma-realm, one would be a deluded person.
Whatever actions or movements there may be, they all do not transcend the mind of the dharma-realm. Why is this? Because the essence of the mind...
This is because it is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Question: Worldly people engage in various studies; why do they not attain the Way? Answer:

It is because of the perception of a self (*ātman*). For this reason, they do not attain the Way. "Self" refers to the ego. The person who has reached the ultimate does not grieve when encountering suffering, nor does he rejoice when encountering pleasure.
Because he does not perceive a self, he does not recognize suffering or pleasure. Because he has extinguished the self, he attains the state of non-substantiality (*śūnyatā*).
If even oneself is already lost, what further thing could possibly not be lost? Question: Since all phenomena (*dharmas*) are empty, who is it that cultivates the Path?
Answer: If there is someone, then one must cultivate the Path; if there is no one, then there is no need to cultivate the Path. "Who" refers to the self (*ātman*).
If there is no self, then upon encountering things, one does not give rise to notions of right and wrong. That which is "right" is simply my own right, while as for things...
It is not so. "Not" means that I myself am not [existent], yet things are not non-existent. When the mind is such that there is no mind, this is called penetrating the Buddha-way.
When one encounters things without giving rise to views, this is named reaching the Way. Encountering things, one directly penetrates them to know their source.
This person’s eye of wisdom has opened. The wise person follows things and does not follow themselves; thus, there is neither grasping nor rejecting, neither opposition nor compliance.

The foolish person follows themselves and does not follow things; thus, there is grasping and rejecting, opposition and compliance. Not seeing a single thing is called "seeing the Way. Not practicing a single thing is called "practicing the Way.
Thus, in all places there is no place, yet this very absence of place is itself the place of action. There is no place of non-action.
By means of the method of practice, one immediately beholds the Buddha. When one perceives the signs (*nimitta*), one sees them in all places;

because ghosts grasp at these signs, they fall into hell, whereas by contemplating the Dharma, one attains liberation. If one perceives conceptualization and discrimination (*vikalpa*), one immediately undergoes such things as the boiling cauldrons and glowing coals, manifesting the signs of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
If one perceives the nature of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), that is the nature of *nirvāṇa*, free from conceptualization and discrimination.
This is precisely the nature of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Because the mind is not form (*rūpa*), it is not existent; because its function is never abandoned, it is not non-existent.
Furthermore, because it functions while being eternally empty, it is not existent; because it is empty while functioning constantly, it is not non-existent.
In the past, while perusing the ancestral lamps, I came upon the biography of Master Dazhu, which mentions a work titled *The Essential Gate for Sudden Enlightenment into the Way* in one fascicle.
I have long admired it, yet my wish had not been fulfilled. Later, in the year of Jiyou (1369) during the Hongwu era, I found an old volume among some discarded boxes.
Opening it at random, I read through several sections; it was like finding coolness when one is parched with heat.

Leaping for joy, he could not contain himself; he then looked at its head and saw that it was this very treatise. He further examined it in detail and scrutinized its principles, finding them straightforward, authentic, and grounded in reality.
It was like drinking the finest clarified butter (*sarpis*) or obtaining a supreme treasure. Later, when he compared it with other records, he found it to be free from error or discrepancy.
Having finally attained what he had sought, he did not dare to keep it secret for himself, but vowed to share it with all beings.

All living beings alike partake of the flavor of the Dharma; furthermore, I have appended at the end a single volume of recorded sayings (*yulu*) concerning the inquiries of various schools, divided briefly into upper and lower sections to form one fascicle, along with the Great Master Bodhidharma’s "Dharma Gate of Settling the Mind" attached to the end of the scroll.

It is collectively titled *The Essential Gate of Sudden Enlightenment*. I have respectfully donated silk and cloth, commissioned artisans to embroider and carve it into woodblocks, so that it may endure imperishably and circulate throughout the ten directions, enabling all practitioners of the Buddha-way under heaven to each clearly understand the path of correct cultivation.
May none fall into false views; may they all suddenly awaken to their own minds and fully open to the Buddha-wisdom. This truly accords with my original vows.

Postscript: Previously, while reading the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) up to the section on Chan Master Dazhu Huihai, I observed how, from his initial meeting with Mazu and his skillful words in guiding others,
through to his general responses to inquiries from various schools that left them tongue-tied and dispirited, he inspired joy in their hearts and won their sincere submission.
I have never ceased to rejoice in this, for the Master’s words are fundamentally rooted in the essential tenets of the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras.
Addressing both phenomena and principle, encompassing both essence and function, they elucidate the ultimate pivot of the Dharma.

Whether manifesting killing or giving life, bestowing or withholding, whether acting with spontaneity or in opposition, all movements accord with the Way as they return to the source. Regarding his work, *The Sudden Enlightenment into*...
The *Daoyamen lun* (Treatise on the Essential Gate of the Way) was once widely circulated in the past, yet in recent years it has become exceptionally rare.
Recently, the monk Miaoye of Siming informed me that he had obtained this treatise; subsequently, through his words, I learned that it lay among the broken fragments within my own worn-out bookcase.

How could I dare keep it for private study alone? I am delighted to share it with the monastic community. I have therefore exhausted my own limited skill to prepare it for publication and have had it carved into printing blocks. I pray that...
With a single word, I recognize its essence hereafter. Furthermore, I present the text from the newly carved woodblocks, from the first to the sixth, totaling six folios, to demonstrate it.
Yet, having once tasted a single morsel from the cauldron, what need is there to behold the entire book? Alas! Is this compilation by Dazhu merely language and writing, or is it not?
If one says it is language and writing, the Way is not language and writing; if one says it is not, [it is nonetheless expressed therein].
The texts of the Tripitaka are clearly present before one's eyes; they are all integrated, synthesized, and arrayed as they flow forth from this old man’s breast.
Yet when he previously presented his questions, he claimed, "I do not understand Chan," and asserted that there is not a single dharma to be shown to others.
Look at these words of his—they are truly like the guilty conscience of a thief. It is all a complete fabrication.
My emotions are so agitated that I cannot compose myself; therefore, today I cannot avoid being further smeared with false accusations by others.

Those who read this in the future, if they can immediately seize the essence at Mazu’s words regarding the "great pearl—perfectly round, luminous, penetrating, and free, without obstruction," then the wish-fulfilling gem that reflects all colors will be fully possessed by everyone. If this is not yet the case, [you must continue to strive].
How many are there who remain trapped within their shells and deluded by their own enclosures? Let those who possess the eye atop the crown of their heads try to discern this for themselves.
